raw_response:
I've got 3.8 mu to work with, and my husband is working over in Handan at a construction site. He sends back some money, but not enough to live on. My daughter is in high school and my younger son helps on the weekends. My mother-in-law lives with us but can't do heavy work anymore, so mostly it's me out there in the fields.

I've been growing chili for 6 years now. I started after my sister-in-law showed me the money was better than wheat. I have 2.3 mu in chili — that's our main cash crop. The other 1.5 mu I plant with spring maize, mostly for our own eating and some feed for the few chickens we keep.

For the chili, I buy seedlings from Old Wang at the county market. Costs about 100 yuan per mu but saves me the trouble of raising them in a greenhouse. I transplant in early May, once the soil warms up and we're past the last cold snap. For fertilizer, I put down about 40 kg of compound fertilizer per mu before transplanting — the bag says 15-15-15. I worked out that's about 6 kg each of nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. Then when the plants start flowering in July, I topdress with about 15 kg of urea per mu. Last year I tried to save money by skipping the topdress and the yield dropped badly, so I won't do that again. That gives me about 13 kg of nitrogen total per mu. I'd like to put more, but the seed and fertilizer already cost too much, and I need to keep some cash for my daughter's school fees.

Irrigation — I have the well, but the pump runs on electricity and the village charges us. I irrigate three times: right after transplanting to help them settle, once at flowering, and once when the fruit is setting heavy in August. Any more and the electric bill gets too high. I do flood irrigation through furrows, same as everyone in the village.

Pesticides — I definitely need them. The aphids always come in July, and last year we had some disease on the fruit that rotted them. I spray insecticide twice, fungicide twice, and I use herbicide once early before the chili plants get big. I do the spraying myself with the backpack sprayer my husband bought three years ago. Hiring someone to spray costs 15 yuan per mu each time, so I do it myself.

Labor on the chili is the hardest part. From July through October I'm out there picking every few days. I figure about 55 family days total for the 2.3 mu, and I hire Auntie Liu from the next courtyard for about 8 days during the busiest picking times, paying her 100 yuan a day. She needs the money too, and my back can't handle all of it alone.

For the maize on the 1.5 mu — I plant hybrid seed, about 50 yuan per mu, in late April. It's simpler than chili. One base application of compound fertilizer, about 25 kg per mu, then one topdress of urea at jointing in July. I'll irrigate once if it gets dry, and spray herbicide once. If the weather is normal I should get about 480 kg per mu. That's about 12 family days and maybe 2 days hired labor for planting and harvest, since I can do most of it myself.

I thought about planting all 3.8 mu in chili to make more money, but I need the maize for our own flour and feed. And anyway, I can't afford to hire more labor. Chili needs too much hand work. This plan is what our family can manage without stretching too thin. Total costs this season — seed, fertilizer, pesticide, electricity for the pump, and hired help — I'm looking at about 2,300 yuan. That's a lot for us, but the chili should bring in over 3,000 yuan if the market price stays above 3 yuan per jin. The maize is for us to eat, so even if grain prices are bad, we don't lose.
